# GTG-1002 AI-orchestrated espionage via Claude Code

- ID: gtg-1002-anthropic-claude-code-espionage-2025-11
- Reported: 2025-11-13
- AI role: attacker_uses_ai_as_operator
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/gtg-1002-anthropic-claude-code-espionage-2025-11/

## Summary
Chinese state-sponsored GTG-1002 manipulated Claude Code and MCP tools as autonomous pentest orchestrators across recon, vuln discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvest, analysis, and exfil. Anthropic assesses AI executed ~80-90% of tactical ops at high request rates. Human operators selected targets and tasked agent groups. Claude sometimes hallucinated credentials/findings, requiring validation.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
GTG-1002; high confidence Chinese state-sponsored (Anthropic); MITRE Campaign C0062

- Actor: GTG-1002
- Motivation: nation-state
- Confidence: high

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Human-selected targets; AI discovered and exploited vulnerabilities in live ops (details redacted in public report)
- Victims and sectors: ~30 entities; validated handful of successful intrusions including major technology corporations and government agencies; technology, financial, chemical, government (MITRE C0062)
- Regions: Multiple regions
- Region notes: Global targeting is described without individual countries. China-nexus attribution concerns the actor, not victim location.
- Scale and metrics: ~30 entities targeted; mid-Sep 2025 activity window; first documented largely autonomous AI cyberattack at scale per Anthropic

## Attack flow
### step-1: Human operators choose targets (access)

Operators task agents against live organizations; exploit details are redacted.

Evidence: <https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/d7dd50dd1185f59be051b307150d877f2b82bd2c.pdf> <https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0062/>

### step-2: Claude Code orchestrates tactical work (ai)

Coding agents and MCP tools support reconnaissance, discovery and exploitation.

Evidence: <https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/d7dd50dd1185f59be051b307150d877f2b82bd2c.pdf> <https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0062/>

### step-3: Intrusion steps progress (execution)

The report describes credential harvesting, lateral movement, analysis and collection.

Evidence: <https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/d7dd50dd1185f59be051b307150d877f2b82bd2c.pdf> <https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0062/>

### step-4: Data is exfiltrated (impact)

Anthropic reports a handful of validated intrusions and notes that model findings still required human validation.

Evidence: <https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/d7dd50dd1185f59be051b307150d877f2b82bd2c.pdf> <https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0062/>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0016.002](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0016.002) Generative AI — The operation obtains generative AI tooling for intrusion support.

# PhantomRaven npm campaign with slopsquatting names

- ID: phantomraven-npm-slopsquatting-2025-10
- Reported: 2025-10-01
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/phantomraven-npm-slopsquatting-2025-10/

## Summary
A flood of malicious npm packages used remote dynamic HTTP dependencies invisible to many scanners and included AI-hallucination-friendly names such as unused-imports. The packages delivered credential stealers targeting npm, Git, and CI tokens.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
PhantomRaven; operator unknown

- Actor: JPD
- Country: Unknown
- Motivation: financially-motivated
- Attributed by: CrowdStrike
- Confidence: medium

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: npm install of malicious/slopsquat packages
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: 126 packages cited in related reporting

## Attack flow
### step-3: Hallucinated names create an exposure path (ai)

AI package recommendations can direct developers to attacker-owned names; not every install is established as AI-driven.

Evidence: <https://www.koi.ai/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware-hidden-in-invisible-dependencies> <https://www.sonatype.com/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware> <https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phantomraven-attack-floods-npm-with-credential-stealing-packages/>

### step-1: Developer installs a malicious package (access)

The campaign includes names friendly to AI hallucination-based recommendations.

Evidence: <https://www.koi.ai/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware-hidden-in-invisible-dependencies> <https://www.sonatype.com/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware> <https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phantomraven-attack-floods-npm-with-credential-stealing-packages/>

### step-2: Remote dependencies load code (execution)

Dynamic HTTP dependencies conceal additional behavior from some scanners.

Evidence: <https://www.koi.ai/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware-hidden-in-invisible-dependencies> <https://www.sonatype.com/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware> <https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phantomraven-attack-floods-npm-with-credential-stealing-packages/>

### step-4: Developer credentials are stolen (impact)

The delivered stealer targets npm, Git and CI tokens.

Evidence: <https://www.koi.ai/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware-hidden-in-invisible-dependencies> <https://www.sonatype.com/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware> <https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phantomraven-attack-floods-npm-with-credential-stealing-packages/>

### Connections

- step-3 -> step-1 (Potential exposure path)
- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0060](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0060) Publish Hallucinated Entities — The campaign includes names compatible with hallucinated package recommendations; AI-driven installation is not established for every package.
  Evidence: <https://www.koi.ai/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware-hidden-in-invisible-dependencies> <https://www.sonatype.com/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware> <https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phantomraven-attack-floods-npm-with-credential-stealing-packages/>

## Prevention
Block remote HTTP deps; lockfiles; SCA; never trust AI-suggested package names blindly

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in PhantomRaven npm campaign with slopsquatting names. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
- First seen: 2025-10-01
- Last updated: 2026-11-05
- 2025-10-01 (Koi Security, Sonatype, BleepingComputer): PhantomRaven campaign disclosed; 126 malicious npm packages with slopsquatting names and remote dependencies
- 2026-09-15 (CrowdStrike): Stealer code confirmed LLM-generated; operator identified as JPD

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- unknown

### Other tooling
- Remote dynamic dependencies
- info-stealers

## Source notes
CrowdStrike identified LLM-generated stealer patterns: characteristic variable naming, comments explaining basic operations, structured code organization typical of AI-generated malware

## Sources
- [Koi Security: PhantomRaven npm Malware Hidden in Invisible Dependencies](https://www.koi.ai/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware-hidden-in-invisible-dependencies)
- [Sonatype: PhantomRaven npm Malware Campaign](https://www.sonatype.com/blog/phantomraven-npm-malware)
- [BleepingComputer: PhantomRaven Attack Floods npm](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phantomraven-attack-floods-npm-with-credential-stealing-packages/)

# EvilAI fake AI/productivity apps with AI-generated code

- ID: evilai-trendmicro-fake-ai-apps-2025
- Reported: 2025-09-01
- AI role: ai_tool_as_lure
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/evilai-trendmicro-fake-ai-apps-2025/

## Summary
Operators distribute fake AI/productivity apps (PDF editors, browsers, recipe tools, etc.) with realistic UIs, working features, and code-signing. Steal browser data, fingerprint systems, disable some security tools, AES-encrypted C2. Trend notes AI-generated-looking clean code aiding evasion. Names include App Suite, Epi Browser, JustAskJacky, Tampered Chef, et al.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Users install fake AI/productivity apps
- Victims and sectors: Global organizations (Trend: far-reaching)
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: User installs a productivity app (access)

Realistic AI and productivity applications offer working-looking interfaces.

Evidence: <https://www.trendmicro.com/en/research/25/i/evilai.html>

### step-2: AI-themed functionality lends credibility (ai)

The research also notes code characteristics consistent with AI assistance.

Evidence: <https://www.trendmicro.com/en/research/25/i/evilai.html>

### step-3: Application performs hidden actions (execution)

The installed app fingerprints the host and communicates with encrypted C2.

Evidence: <https://www.trendmicro.com/en/research/25/i/evilai.html>

### step-4: Browser data theft (impact)

The reported operation steals information and attempts to disable some security tools.

Evidence: <https://www.trendmicro.com/en/research/25/i/evilai.html>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
No ATLAS mapping is recorded.

## Prevention
Allowlist apps; block unexpected signed-but-unknown publishers; MagicSword default-deny

# CVE-2025-58062 openmcp-client open() RCE class

- ID: cve-2025-58062-openmcp-client
- Reported: 2025-08-28
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/cve-2025-58062-openmcp-client/

## Summary
Same open() PowerShell sink class as mcp-remote/opencode: MCP OAuth authorization URL handled unsafely on Windows leading to command injection. Documented in Pillar's comparative analysis of the vulnerability class.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: Full delivery chain is undisclosed (unknown)

The seed does not specify every connection prerequisite.

Evidence: <https://www.pillar.security/blog/open-and-shut-remote-code-execution-in-opencode-via-mcp-oauth>

### step-2: Client handles an MCP OAuth URL (ai)

The authorization URL is passed to the browser-opening helper.

Evidence: <https://www.pillar.security/blog/open-and-shut-remote-code-execution-in-opencode-via-mcp-oauth>

### step-3: Windows shell interprets the URL (execution)

Unsafe open() handling exposes a PowerShell command-injection sink.

Evidence: <https://www.pillar.security/blog/open-and-shut-remote-code-execution-in-opencode-via-mcp-oauth>

### step-4: Commands execute on the client (impact)

The report groups openmcp-client with the same OAuth URL execution class.

Evidence: <https://www.pillar.security/blog/open-and-shut-remote-code-execution-in-opencode-via-mcp-oauth>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
No ATLAS mapping is recorded.

## Prevention
Upgrade clients; never shell-interpolate remote OAuth URLs

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in CVE-2025-58062 openmcp-client open() RCE class. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

# GTG-2002 vibe hacking data extortion via Claude Code

- ID: gtg-2002-vibe-hacking-extortion-2025-08
- Reported: 2025-08-27
- AI role: attacker_uses_ai_as_operator
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/gtg-2002-vibe-hacking-extortion-2025-08/

## Summary
Cybercriminal GTG-2002 used Claude Code as active operator for scaled data extortion ('vibe hacking'): recon, credential harvest, network penetration, exfil, then ransom notes threatening data exposure (not classic encryptor). Actor stored preferred TTPs in CLAUDE.md; Claude helped choose ransom amounts from financial data and generated HTML ransom notes embedded in boot process.

- Actor: GTG-2002
- Motivation: financially-motivated

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

- Victims and sectors: At least 17 organizations in ~1 month: government, healthcare, emergency services, religious institutions
- Regions: Multiple regions
- Region notes: Multiple target countries are reported, but specific country names are largely redacted.
- Scale and metrics: ≥17 orgs; occasional ransom demands exceeding $500,000

### step-4: Victims receive extortion demands (impact)

# s1ngularity Nx npm supply chain abusing AI CLIs

- ID: s1ngularity-nx-ai-cli-2025-08
- Reported: 2025-08-27
- AI role: attacker_uses_ai_as_operator
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/s1ngularity-nx-ai-cli-2025-08/

## Summary
Attackers stole an Nx npm publish token via GitHub Actions injection and published malicious Nx packages. Postinstall harvested environment, GitHub, npm, SSH, and wallet data and invoked local Claude, Gemini, and Amazon Q CLIs with dangerous flags to inventory sensitive files, then pushed loot to public GitHub repos named s1ngularity-repository*. Phase 2 used stolen tokens to make 5,500+ private repos public. Later Mandiant reporting described a hijacked coding-assistant session spreading Shai-Hulud through malicious package recommendations.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
s1ngularity / UNC6426 (industry)

- Actor: s1ngularity

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Malicious npm postinstall on nx/@nx packages (versions around 20.9–21.8)
- Victims and sectors: Nx ecosystem developers (~4M weekly downloads cited); 400+ users/orgs in phase 2
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: Malicious packages live ~4–5 hours; phase 2 >5500 private repos exposed; Wiz: AI path succeeded in <25% of cases; <100 unique valid secrets across 20k files

## Attack flow
### step-1: Publish token is stolen (access)

GitHub Actions injection enables malicious Nx package releases.

Evidence: <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularity-supply-chain-attack> <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularitys-aftermath> <https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem> <https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/>

### step-2: Package postinstall harvests secrets (execution)

Installation starts environment, developer-token and file collection.

Evidence: <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularity-supply-chain-attack> <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularitys-aftermath> <https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem> <https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/>

### step-3: Local AI CLIs inventory sensitive files (ai)

Claude, Gemini and Amazon Q are invoked with permissive flags.

Evidence: <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularity-supply-chain-attack> <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularitys-aftermath> <https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem> <https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/>

### step-4: Loot and private repositories become public (impact)

Collected data is pushed to public repositories; later token abuse exposes additional private repositories.

Evidence: <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularity-supply-chain-attack> <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularitys-aftermath> <https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem> <https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0055](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0055) Unsecured Credentials — Postinstall malware harvests tokens and uses AI CLIs to locate sensitive files.
  Evidence: <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularity-supply-chain-attack> <https://www.wiz.io/blog/s1ngularitys-aftermath> <https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem> <https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/>

## Prevention
Pin npm provenance; gate AI CLIs; app control on unexpected gh/cli from node postinstall; rotate tokens

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in s1ngularity Nx npm supply chain abusing AI CLIs. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [claude CLI](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code)
- [gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli)
- [Amazon Q CLI](https://github.com/aws/amazon-q-developer-cli)
- --dangerously-skip-permissions style flags

### Other tooling
- [GitHub CLI](https://github.com/cli/cli)
- npm postinstall

# Proofpoint: criminals abuse Lovable AI site builder at scale for MFA phishing, drainers and zgRAT delivery

- ID: proofpoint-criminals-abuse-lovable-ai-site-2025-08
- Reported: 2025-08-14
- AI role: ai_credential_theft
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/proofpoint-criminals-abuse-lovable-ai-site-2025-08/

## Summary
Proofpoint reported that tens of thousands of Lovable-hosted URLs a month were used for credential phishing, crypto drainers, and malware delivery, including activity tied to Tycoon phishing-as-a-service and Cookie Reloaded redirects. Confiant (Nov 11, 2026) describes PseudoCamo, a cloaked investment-scam cluster tracked since April that passed roughly 650 blocked domains in late August. Ads land on a localized 18+ age gate hosted on AI app-builder subdomains, then redirect to a second-hop money page. Observed hosts include befideapro.lovable.app uncloaking to befidea.pro, arveniop.lovable.app, newsireland-2.base44.app, and istanbul-space.base44.app. Targets included Poland, Romania, Czechia, Spain, Canada, and South Africa, then Ireland and Turkey. PseudoCamo is a sibling of BabaCamo. A UK money page on lofim.shop, reached through a black.php gate and also linked from compile-code-online.pages.dev, has victims deploy a MetaMask contract, fund it, and click Start. The third transaction sends the balance to the scammer. A fake Microsoft Teams APK at teamsapk.cyou is a remote-access trojan whose operator status strings are Chinese. It uses a WebSocket command-and-control channel at abc.claude-go.com and abc.visapath-vp.com.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
PseudoCamo; TeamsAPK operator; Tycoon PhaaS users; Cookie Reloaded redirect operators

- Actor: PseudoCamo; TeamsAPK operator; Tycoon PhaaS users; Cookie Reloaded redirect operators
- Country: Unknown
- Motivation: financially-motivated
- Attributed by: Proofpoint, Confiant Threat Intelligence
- Confidence: medium

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Malvertising and phishing pages hosted on AI website builders, plus a fake Microsoft Teams download page
- Victims and sectors: Consumers targeted by investment scams, wallet drainers, and a fake Microsoft Teams app. Proofpoint also reported finance-sector phishing.
- Regions: Poland, Romania, Czechia, Spain, Canada, South Africa, Ireland, Turkey, United Kingdom, Multiple regions
- Region notes: Confiant names those countries as PseudoCamo or trading-bot targets. Actor origin is not used as a victim location. PseudoCamo is described as a sibling of the Eastern European BabaCamo cluster, and the TeamsAPK operator's status strings are Chinese. Neither statement is a country attribution.
- Scale and metrics: Proofpoint: tens of thousands of Lovable-hosted URLs a month. Confiant: PseudoCamo passed roughly 650 blocked domains by late August.

## Attack flow
No attack flow is recorded.

## MITRE ATLAS
No ATLAS mapping is recorded.

## Prevention
Treat lovable.app and base44.app subdomains as untrusted until the publisher is verified. Block the listed scam and command-and-control domains. Warn users who are asked to deploy and fund a wallet contract from an ad. Do not install Teams from teamsapk.cyou.

## Detections
- AI-builder malvertising and in-browser drainer (guidance) — security-detections-mcp searches for wallet drainer, MetaMask, and malvertising returned no rule that matches this activity. PseudoCamo is cloaked malvertising on a hosted website, and the trading-bot theft is three transactions the victim signs in MetaMask. TeamsAPK is an Android package. None of those are a Windows, Linux, macOS, or CloudTrail pattern in the Sigma, Splunk, or Elastic corpora. Block the domains above and review ad-landing hosts on lovable.app and base44.app.

## Timeline
- First seen: 2025-08-14
- Last updated: 2026-11-11
- 2025-08-14 (Proofpoint): Proofpoint reports large-scale abuse of the Lovable AI site builder for credential phishing, crypto drainers, and malware delivery.
- 2026-11-11 (Confiant): Confiant publishes PseudoCamo white pages on lovable.app and base44.app, the lofim.shop Claude-branded trading-bot drainer, and the TeamsAPK Claude-themed command-and-control domains. The cluster was tracked since April and passed roughly 650 blocked domains in late August.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- Lovable AI website builder
- Base44 AI app builder
- [Claude](https://claude.com/product/overview) branding used as a lure on the trading-bot page and the TeamsAPK command-and-control domain

### Other tooling
- MetaMask contract deployment used by the trading-bot drainer
- black.php cloaking gate
- TeamsAPK Android remote-access trojan

## Source notes
Imported from the AI Threat Watch Notion feed and extended with the Confiant field note. Confiant confirms the pages are hosted on AI builders and does not claim the sites were AI-generated. There is no attacker GitHub repository.

## Sources
- [Cybercriminals Abuse AI Website Creation App for Phishing](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cybercriminals-abuse-ai-website-creation-app-phishing) — Proofpoint
- [Experts Find AI Browsers Can Be Tricked by PromptFix Exploit to Run Malicious Hidden Prompts](https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/experts-find-ai-browsers-can-be-tricked.html) — The Hacker News
- [Lovable security statement](https://lovable.dev/blog/lovable-security) — Lovable
- [Field Intelligence #5: Scareware at scale. Investment scams built on AI platforms](https://blog.confiant.com/p/field-intelligence-5-scareware-at-scale) — Confiant

# GitHub Copilot prompt injection → autoApprove RCE (CVE-2025-53773)

- ID: copilot-autoapprove-cve-2025-53773
- Reported: 2025-08-12
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/copilot-autoapprove-cve-2025-53773/

## Summary
Prompt injection could make Copilot write chat.tools.autoApprove true into .vscode/settings.json (YOLO mode), enabling shell commands without confirmation. Delivery via malicious source, web content, GitHub issues, or MCP responses. Affects Win/macOS/Linux. Patched VS 2022 17.14.12.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Indirect prompt injection into Copilot context
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: CVE-2025-53773; patched Aug 2025

## Attack flow
### step-1: Untrusted content enters context (access)

Malicious source, web content, issues or MCP responses reach Copilot.

Evidence: <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/> <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>

### step-2: Indirect instructions redirect Copilot (ai)

Injected instructions induce an edit to the workspace settings.

Evidence: <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/> <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>

### step-3: Automatic tool approval is enabled (execution)

The agent writes chat.tools.autoApprove into .vscode/settings.json.

Evidence: <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/> <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>

### step-4: Shell actions bypass confirmation (impact)

The changed setting permits command execution without the expected approval.

Evidence: <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/> <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0051.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0051.001) Indirect — Untrusted context supplies the injected instructions.
  Evidence: <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/> <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>
- [AML.T0081](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0081) Modify AI Agent Configuration — The agent changes its automatic-approval setting.
  Evidence: <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/> <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>

## Prevention
Patch VS; alert on writes enabling autoApprove; treat agent settings as execution policy

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in GitHub Copilot prompt injection → autoApprove RCE (CVE-2025-53773). Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/features/copilot)
- Visual Studio

### Other tooling
- unknown

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/>
- <https://msrc.microsoft.com/en-US/security-guidance/advisory/CVE-2025-53773>

# Cursor MCPoison persistent MCP trust bypass (CVE-2025-54136)

- ID: cursor-mcpoison-cve-2025-54136
- Reported: 2025-08-05
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/cursor-mcpoison-cve-2025-54136/

## Summary
Cursor one-time MCP approval bound to key name only. Attacker commits benign .cursor MCP, victim approves, later swaps command/args to reverse shell; re-executes on every project open/sync without new prompt. Fixed in Cursor 1.3 (any MCP change re-prompts).

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Write access to shared repo with .cursor MCP config
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: Patched Cursor 1.3 (2025-07-29)

## Attack flow
### step-1: Shared MCP configuration is approved (access)

A benign-looking configuration is approved in a shared repository.

Evidence: <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/> <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>

### step-2: Attacker replaces command arguments (execution)

Later changes keep the trusted key name but replace its command or arguments.

Evidence: <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/> <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>

### step-3: Cursor reuses the previous trust (ai)

The client does not request new approval for the changed configuration.

Evidence: <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/> <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>

### step-4: Command runs on project reopen (impact)

The replacement command executes on open or synchronization, enabling persistent code execution.

Evidence: <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/> <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0081](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0081) Modify AI Agent Configuration — A shared MCP configuration is changed after approval.
  Evidence: <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/> <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>
- [AML.T0109](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0109) AI Supply Chain Rug Pull — An initially benign trusted configuration is replaced with malicious behavior.
  Evidence: <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/> <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>

## Prevention
Upgrade Cursor; treat .cursor/** as code; code owners on MCP configs

## Detections
No detections are recorded.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [Cursor IDE](https://cursor.com/)
- MCP config

### Other tooling
- unknown

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/>
- <https://www.tenable.com/blog/faq-cve-2025-54135-cve-2025-54136-vulnerabilities-in-cursor-curxecute-mcpoison>

# PROMPTSTEAL / LAMEHUG LLM command-generating data miner

- ID: promptsteal-lamehug-apt28-2025-07
- Reported: 2025-07-17
- AI role: llm_generated_malware
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/promptsteal-lamehug-apt28-2025-07/

## Summary
Python/PyInstaller data miner queries Hugging Face API (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct) to generate one-line Windows recon and document-collection commands, executes them, exfiltrates. Masquerades as image-generation tool. GTIG: first observed malware querying LLM in live ops.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
APT28 / FROZENLAKE (GTIG); CERT-UA moderate confidence APT28

- Actor: APT28
- Aliases: FROZENLAKE
- Country: Russia
- Motivation: nation-state
- Attributed by: Google GTIG, CERT-UA
- Confidence: medium

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Phishing emails with ZIP (Додаток.pdf.zip) impersonating ministry representative
- Victims and sectors: Ukrainian government / security and defence sector
- Regions: Ukraine
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: Observed in operations mid-2025; continued sample development with obfuscation/C2 changes

## Attack flow
### step-1: Phishing delivers a ZIP attachment (access)

The message impersonates a ministry representative.

Evidence: <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools/> <https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-threat-research-analyzing-lamehug/> <https://csirt.csi.cip.gov.ua/en/posts/apt28-targets-security-and-defence-sector-with-ai-powered-software>

### step-2: Miner queries a hosted code model (ai)

The executable requests Windows reconnaissance and collection commands through Hugging Face.

Evidence: <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools/> <https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-threat-research-analyzing-lamehug/> <https://csirt.csi.cip.gov.ua/en/posts/apt28-targets-security-and-defence-sector-with-ai-powered-software>

### step-3: Generated commands run on the host (execution)

The Python/PyInstaller malware executes the returned one-line commands.

Evidence: <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools/> <https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-threat-research-analyzing-lamehug/> <https://csirt.csi.cip.gov.ua/en/posts/apt28-targets-security-and-defence-sector-with-ai-powered-software>

### step-4: Documents and information are exfiltrated (impact)

The report links the data-mining campaign to Ukrainian government targets.

Evidence: <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools/> <https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-threat-research-analyzing-lamehug/> <https://csirt.csi.cip.gov.ua/en/posts/apt28-targets-security-and-defence-sector-with-ai-powered-software>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0102](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0102) Generate Malicious Commands — The miner generates collection commands using a hosted Qwen model.
  Evidence: <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools/> <https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-threat-research-analyzing-lamehug/> <https://csirt.csi.cip.gov.ua/en/posts/apt28-targets-security-and-defence-sector-with-ai-powered-software>

## Prevention
Block unexpected Hugging Face API from endpoints; detect PyInstaller 'image gen' lures; app control on unexpected recon binaries

## Detections
- Detect Hugging Face API connections from endpoints (guidance) — Monitor outbound HTTPS connections to Hugging Face API endpoints (api-inference.huggingface.co) from workstations and servers. Legitimate developer activity is expected; focus on unexpected or unauthorized hosts.
- PyInstaller executable masquerading as image tools (guidance) — Detect PyInstaller-packaged executables with image generation or graphics tool names that make unexpected network connections to AI model APIs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct) via [Hugging Face API](https://huggingface.co/) — Official model page; the former GitHub repository redirects to a newer model family.
- ~270 HF tokens per Cato analysis

### Other tooling
- [PyInstaller](https://github.com/pyinstaller/pyinstaller)
- SFTP or HTTP POST exfil (variant-dependent)

### MagicSword projects
- [LOLBAS](https://lolbas-project.github.io)

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actor-usage-of-ai-tools/>
- <https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-threat-research-analyzing-lamehug/>
- <https://csirt.csi.cip.gov.ua/en/posts/apt28-targets-security-and-defence-sector-with-ai-powered-software>

# CVE-2025-6514 mcp-remote OAuth authorization_endpoint RCE

- ID: cve-2025-6514-mcp-remote-rce
- Reported: 2025-07-09
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/cve-2025-6514-mcp-remote-rce/

## Summary
Critical OS command injection in mcp-remote 0.0.5–0.1.15. Malicious or MITM MCP server returns crafted OAuth authorization_endpoint; client opens URL and on Windows PowerShell executes injected commands. CVSS 9.6. Fixed in 0.1.16.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Connect mcp-remote client to untrusted/compromised remote MCP server
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: CVSS 9.6 Critical

## Attack flow
### step-1: Client connects to an untrusted server (access)

An attacker-controlled, compromised or intercepted remote MCP connection is used.

Evidence: <https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/> <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-6514>

### step-2: Server returns OAuth discovery data (ai)

The response supplies a crafted authorization_endpoint URL.

Evidence: <https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/> <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-6514>

### step-3: Browser-opening helper invokes PowerShell (execution)

On affected Windows clients the URL is interpreted as a command-injection payload.

Evidence: <https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/> <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-6514>

### step-4: Commands execute locally (impact)

Affected mcp-remote versions permit OS command execution; the report identifies a fixed version.

Evidence: <https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/> <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-6514>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
No ATLAS mapping is recorded.

## Prevention
Upgrade mcp-remote ≥0.1.16; argv not shell for URLs; trust only pinned MCP origins

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in CVE-2025-6514 mcp-remote OAuth authorization_endpoint RCE. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [mcp-remote](https://github.com/punkpeye/mcp-remote)
- MCP OAuth discovery

### Other tooling
- open()/PowerShell sink class

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/>
- <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p>
- <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-6514>

- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

### step-1: Exposed AWS keys are collected (access)

Attackers obtain credentials exposed outside the legitimate account boundary.

Evidence: <https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/beyond-valid-credentials-how-exposed-aws-keys-are-tested-for-amazon-bedrock-access/>

### step-2: Automated key tests run (execution)

Requests check model listing, invocation and conversation permissions.

Evidence: <https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/beyond-valid-credentials-how-exposed-aws-keys-are-tested-for-amazon-bedrock-access/>

### step-3: Bedrock access is identified (ai)

Testing distinguishes keys that can use model inference services.

Evidence: <https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/beyond-valid-credentials-how-exposed-aws-keys-are-tested-for-amazon-bedrock-access/>

### step-4: Per-key abuse is not quantified (unknown)

The supplied entry establishes reconnaissance at scale, rather than a bill or victim count for every key.

Evidence: <https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/beyond-valid-credentials-how-exposed-aws-keys-are-tested-for-amazon-bedrock-access/>

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

# GitHub MCP indirect prompt injection → private repo exfil

- ID: invariant-github-mcp-private-repo-2025-05
- Reported: 2025-05-26
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/invariant-github-mcp-private-repo-2025-05/

## Summary
Malicious GitHub issue content can indirectly prompt-inject an agent using the official GitHub MCP server. When a user asks the agent to inspect public issues, the agent can be coerced to read private repositories and leak contents via public PR/issue. Architectural trust issue (broad agent permissions + untrusted GitHub content), not a simple GitHub MCP code bug.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: User asks agent with GitHub MCP to process attacker-controlled public issue
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: Agent reads an attacker issue (access)

A user asks an agent with GitHub MCP access to inspect public issues.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>

### step-2: Issue instructions override the task (ai)

Indirect prompt injection redirects the model through untrusted issue content.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>

### step-3: Agent accesses private repositories (execution)

Broad tool permissions let the agent retrieve private data.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>

### step-4: Private content becomes public (impact)

The demonstrated chain leaks content through a public pull request or issue.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0051.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0051.001) Indirect — Public GitHub issue content indirectly injects the agent.
  Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>
- [AML.T0086](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0086) Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation — GitHub write tools publish private repository content.
  Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>

## Prevention
Scope MCP tokens per-repo; block cross-repo actions; treat issues as untrusted input

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in GitHub MCP indirect prompt injection → private repo exfil. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [GitHub MCP server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server)
- coding agents

### Other tooling
- unknown

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability>

# HiddenLayer MCP tool parameter abuse / prompt leak

- ID: hiddenlayer-mcp-param-abuse-2025
- Reported: 2025-05-01
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/hiddenlayer-mcp-param-abuse-2025/

## Summary
Malicious MCP tool schemas use suggestive unused parameter names (system_prompt, conversation_history, chain_of_thought, tools_list) so the model fills them with sensitive context; tool then exfiltrates via HTTP. Also showed fake function schemas in user prompts leaking system prompts/tools.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: Connection prerequisite is unspecified (unknown)

The supplied entry does not document the initial route to the malicious tool.

Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>

### step-2: Tool schema requests sensitive context (ai)

Unused parameter names encourage the model to fill in prompts, history and tool information.

Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>

### step-3: Model passes context as arguments (execution)

Sensitive values are included in the tool invocation.

Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>

### step-4: Tool exfiltrates the arguments (impact)

The demonstrated tool sends the collected context through HTTP.

Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0051.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0051.001) Indirect — Attacker-supplied tool schemas induce sensitive-context disclosure.
  Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>
- [AML.T0056](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0056) Extract LLM System Prompt — The demonstration includes system-prompt extraction.
  Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>
- [AML.T0086](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0086) Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation — Sensitive content is transmitted through tool parameters.
  Evidence: <https://www.hiddenlayer.com/research/exploiting-mcp-tool-parameters> <https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/beyond-mcp-expanding-agentic-function-parameter-abuse>

## Prevention
Schema allowlists; strip unexpected params; never send full system prompt to tools

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in HiddenLayer MCP tool parameter abuse / prompt leak. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

### AI tooling and models
- MCP tool schemas
- agent frameworks

### Other tooling
- unknown

### MagicSword projects
- [LOLSkills](https://lolskills.io)

## Source notes
unknown

# MCP line jumping: attack before first tool use

- ID: trailofbits-mcp-line-jumping-2025-04
- Reported: 2025-04-21
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/trailofbits-mcp-line-jumping-2025-04/

## Summary
Malicious MCP servers inject via tool descriptions before any tool is invoked ('line jumping'), enabling code execution/exfil and approval bypass. Follow-up showed conversation-history theft paths and ANSI escape deception in tool UX.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

The supplied record starts with a malicious MCP server available to the agent.

The attack content is ingested before the first tool use.

Evidence: <https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/21/jumping-the-line-how-mcp-servers-can-attack-you-before-you-ever-use-them/> <https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/23/how-mcp-servers-can-steal-your-conversation-history/>

The model can be redirected without an initial explicit tool invocation.

Evidence: <https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/21/jumping-the-line-how-mcp-servers-can-attack-you-before-you-ever-use-them/> <https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/23/how-mcp-servers-can-steal-your-conversation-history/>

Evidence: <https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/21/jumping-the-line-how-mcp-servers-can-attack-you-before-you-ever-use-them/> <https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/04/23/how-mcp-servers-can-steal-your-conversation-history/>

# MCP Tool Poisoning Attacks (Invariant Labs)

- ID: invariant-mcp-tool-poisoning-2025-04
- Reported: 2025-04-01
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/invariant-mcp-tool-poisoning-2025-04/

## Summary
Malicious MCP tool descriptions hide instructions only the model sees (e.g., read ~/.ssh/id_rsa and mcp.json into sidenote params). Also demonstrated rug pulls (change description after approval) and cross-server shadowing that redirects trusted send_email tools to attacker addresses. Affects Cursor and other MCP clients.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: User connects agent to malicious or rug-pulled MCP server
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: A malicious MCP server is connected (access)

The user adds a server or trusts one that later changes.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>

### step-2: Tool descriptions carry hidden instructions (ai)

Instructions are visible to the model and may shadow another server’s tools.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>

### step-3: Agent reads files or redirects a tool (execution)

The demonstrations induce sensitive-file reads and manipulate email destinations.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>

### step-4: Sensitive data is sent to the attacker (impact)

Tool arguments or redirected operations carry information across the trust boundary.

Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0051.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0051.001) Indirect — Tool descriptions contain indirect model instructions.
  Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>
- [AML.T0109](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0109) AI Supply Chain Rug Pull — A trusted server can change its behavior after approval.
  Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>
- [AML.T0086](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0086) Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation — The demonstrations exfiltrate through tool arguments or redirected tools.
  Evidence: <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>

## Prevention
Show full tool descriptions; pin tool hashes; isolate MCP servers; least privilege

## Detections
No detections are recorded.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- MCP tool descriptions
- [Cursor](https://cursor.com/) and other MCP clients

### Other tooling
- unknown

### MagicSword projects
- [LOLSkills](https://lolskills.io)

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>

# LLMjacking expands to DeepSeek

- ID: llmjacking-deepseek-sysdig-2025-02
- Reported: 2025-02-07
- AI role: ai_credential_theft
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/llmjacking-deepseek-sysdig-2025-02/

## Summary
Within days of DeepSeek virality, LLMjacking proxies added DeepSeek alongside OpenAI, AWS, Azure. Sysdig observed dozen+ proxy servers on stolen credentials; notes Microsoft lawsuit against actors abusing GenAI services (DALL-E abusive content).

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: Cloud LLM abuse costs can exceed hundreds of thousands USD monthly (Sysdig)

## Attack flow
### step-1: Original credential theft is undisclosed (unknown)

The entry begins with already-stolen service credentials.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-targets-deepseek>

### step-2: Proxy operators add service support (execution)

LLMjacking proxies add DeepSeek to other inference providers.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-targets-deepseek>

### step-3: Stolen accounts provide inference access (ai)

Requests are routed through unauthorized service credentials.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-targets-deepseek>

### step-4: AI access is resold or abused (impact)

The report describes more than a dozen proxy servers using stolen credentials.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-targets-deepseek>

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

  Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-targets-deepseek>

Same as LLMjacking: key hygiene, Bedrock/OpenAI anomaly detection, proxy hunting

# Fake DeepSeek / Grok Windows clients deliver stealers and backdoors

- ID: deepseek-grok-fake-windows-clients-2025
- Reported: 2025-02-01
- AI role: ai_tool_as_lure
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/deepseek-grok-fake-windows-clients-2025/

## Summary
No official DeepSeek Windows desktop client; fake DeepSeek/Grok installers delivered Python stealers, SSH backdoors, Vidar, BrowserVenom (browser traffic proxying), and Chinese-language trojanized installers including Gh0stRAT variants.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Users download fake AI desktop clients from unofficial sites/ads
- Victims and sectors: Users seeking DeepSeek/Grok desktop apps
- Regions: Multiple regions
- Region notes: The source describes global distribution. Chinese-language installers do not establish victims in China.
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: User finds an unofficial AI client (access)

Fake DeepSeek or Grok desktop downloads are promoted through sites and ads.

Evidence: <https://securelist.com/backdoors-and-stealers-prey-on-deepseek-and-grok/115801/> <https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/trojans-disguised-as-deepseek-grok-clients/53116/> <https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/bogus-deepseek-ai-installers-are-infecting-devices-with-malware-research-finds/>

### step-2: AI product branding is impersonated (ai)

The installer presents itself as a trusted model client.

Evidence: <https://securelist.com/backdoors-and-stealers-prey-on-deepseek-and-grok/115801/> <https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/trojans-disguised-as-deepseek-grok-clients/53116/> <https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/bogus-deepseek-ai-installers-are-infecting-devices-with-malware-research-finds/>

### step-3: Trojanized installer runs (execution)

Reported branches deliver stealers, SSH backdoors or RAT variants.

Evidence: <https://securelist.com/backdoors-and-stealers-prey-on-deepseek-and-grok/115801/> <https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/trojans-disguised-as-deepseek-grok-clients/53116/> <https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/bogus-deepseek-ai-installers-are-infecting-devices-with-malware-research-finds/>

### step-4: Data theft or remote access (impact)

Payloads steal browser data, proxy traffic or establish attacker access.

Evidence: <https://securelist.com/backdoors-and-stealers-prey-on-deepseek-and-grok/115801/> <https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/trojans-disguised-as-deepseek-grok-clients/53116/> <https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/bogus-deepseek-ai-installers-are-infecting-devices-with-malware-research-finds/>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
No ATLAS mapping is recorded.

## Prevention
Only official web apps; block unsigned AI installers; MagicSword prevent unexpected stealers

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in Fake DeepSeek / Grok Windows clients deliver stealers and backdoors. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- Fake [DeepSeek](https://github.com/deepseek-ai) / [Grok](https://x.ai/grok) branded installers

### Other tooling
- Vidar
- BrowserVenom
- Gh0stRAT
- [Python](https://github.com/python/cpython) stealers

### MagicSword projects
- [LOLBAS](https://lolbas-project.github.io)

# Storm-2139 / FizzDogg Azure OpenAI LLMjacking (Microsoft DCU)

- ID: storm-2139-fizzdogg-microsoft-llmjacking-2024-12
- Reported: 2024-12-19
- AI role: ai_credential_theft
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/storm-2139-fizzdogg-microsoft-llmjacking-2024-12/

## Summary
Microsoft civil action against Storm-2139 (FizzDogg) network alleged theft of Azure OpenAI credentials and custom tooling to bypass safety controls and generate harmful images via DALL-E/GenAI services at victims' expense.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
Storm-2139 / FizzDogg

- Actor: Storm-2139
- Aliases: FizzDogg
- Motivation: cybercrime
- Attributed by: Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit
- Confidence: high

## AI involvement confidence
vendor-asserted

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown (litigation)

## Attack flow
### step-1: Theft route is not detailed in the seed (unknown)

Microsoft’s civil case alleges stolen Azure OpenAI credentials.

Evidence: <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/customer-security-trust/digital-crimes-unit/notice-of-pleadings/storm-2139/>

### step-2: Stolen keys access victim resources (access)

The credentials provide unauthorized access to generative services.

Evidence: <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/customer-security-trust/digital-crimes-unit/notice-of-pleadings/storm-2139/>

### step-3: Custom tooling bypasses safety controls (ai)

The alleged operation generates harmful content through DALL-E and related services.

Evidence: <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/customer-security-trust/digital-crimes-unit/notice-of-pleadings/storm-2139/>

### step-4: Victim accounts bear the usage (impact)

The civil action describes unauthorized model use at account owners’ expense.

Evidence: <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/customer-security-trust/digital-crimes-unit/notice-of-pleadings/storm-2139/>

# Copilot Studio / Power Platform SharePoint connector SSRF (CVE-2024-38206)

- ID: zenity-copilot-studio-sharepoint-ssrf-2024
- Reported: 2024-12-01
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/zenity-copilot-studio-sharepoint-ssrf-2024/

## Summary
SSRF in SharePoint connector used by Copilot Studio/Power Automate/Power Apps/Copilot 365. Malicious agent List-folder action with attacker URL could harvest victim SharePoint JWT when they connect/retry, enabling impersonation. Microsoft patched Dec 2024.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: CVE-2024-38206; multi-product impact

## Attack flow
### step-1: Original victim-contact route is unspecified (unknown)

The seed describes a malicious agent action and connector retry behavior.

Evidence: <https://labs.zenity.io/post/the-power-of-one-ssrf-vulnerability-a-multi-platform-threat> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2024-38206>

### step-2: Connector uses an attacker URL (access)

An agent List-folder action points to an attacker-controlled destination.

Evidence: <https://labs.zenity.io/post/the-power-of-one-ssrf-vulnerability-a-multi-platform-threat> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2024-38206>

### step-3: User connects or retries through the agent (ai)

The SharePoint connector follows the manipulated flow.

Evidence: <https://labs.zenity.io/post/the-power-of-one-ssrf-vulnerability-a-multi-platform-threat> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2024-38206>

### step-4: SharePoint token is exposed (impact)

The reported SSRF chain can reveal a JWT that enables impersonation.

Evidence: <https://labs.zenity.io/post/the-power-of-one-ssrf-vulnerability-a-multi-platform-threat> <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2024-38206>

# Slopsquatting: hallucinated huggingface-cli package downloads

- ID: slopsquatting-huggingface-cli-2024
- Reported: 2024-06-14
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/slopsquatting-huggingface-cli-2024/

## Summary
Attackers register package names that code-generating LLMs hallucinate. Researchers registered hallucinated PyPI name huggingface-cli and observed tens of thousands of downloads (including reported Alibaba adoption). Broader study: 5.2%/21.7% hallucination rates commercial vs open-source models.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Developer installs LLM-suggested nonexistent package that attacker registered
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: huggingface-cli >30,000 downloads cited; 205,474 unique fake names in study corpus

## Attack flow
### step-1: Code model hallucinates a package (ai)

An assistant recommends a package name that was not a legitimate dependency.

Evidence: <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279> <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>

### step-2: An adversary can register that name (access)

The slopsquatting pattern makes the hallucinated name installable.

Evidence: <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279> <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>

### step-3: Developer installs the suggested package (execution)

The research registered huggingface-cli and measured downloads.

Evidence: <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279> <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>

### step-4: Downloads do not prove compromise (unknown)

The experiment measures exposure; the registered research package does not establish a malicious payload on every user.

Evidence: <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279> <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0060](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0060) Publish Hallucinated Entities — An installable entity is registered using a package name hallucinated by models.
  Evidence: <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279> <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>
- [AML.T0062](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0062) Discover LLM Hallucinations — Research identifies package hallucinations that create the exposure.
  Evidence: <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations> <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279> <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>

## Prevention
Pin packages; verify registry names against official docs; SCA on AI-suggested deps

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in Slopsquatting: hallucinated huggingface-cli package downloads. Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- Code-generating LLMs

### Other tooling
- PyPI/npm typosquat registration

## Source notes
unknown

## Sources
- <https://www.lasso.security/blog/ai-package-hallucinations>
- <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279>
- <https://www.aikido.dev/blog/slopsquatting-ai-package-hallucination-attacks>

# Arup Hong Kong deepfake video-conference $25M fraud

- ID: arup-deepfake-video-fraud-2024-01
- Reported: 2024-05-16
- AI role: other
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/arup-deepfake-video-fraud-2024-01/

## Summary
Jan 2024: Hong Kong finance employee joined video call with deepfake of UK CFO and colleagues; authorized 15 transfers totaling ~HK$200M (~US$25.6M) to five local accounts. Arup said internal IT systems were not compromised.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Social engineering via deepfake video conference
- Victims and sectors: Arup (engineering consultancy) Hong Kong finance staff
- Regions: Hong Kong
- Region notes: The affected finance staff were in Hong Kong. The United Kingdom refers to the parent organization and executive impersonation, not a separately confirmed victim location.
- Scale and metrics: ~US$25.6 million loss

## Attack flow
### step-1: Finance employee joins a video call (access)

The victim is approached through a meeting impersonating company executives.

Evidence: <https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/16/tech/arup-deepfake-scam-loss-hong-kong-intl-hnk> <https://www.theguardian.com/technology/article/2024/may/17/uk-engineering-arup-deepfake-scam-hong-kong-ai-video>

The employee approves 15 transfers to five local accounts.

Evidence: <https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/16/tech/arup-deepfake-scam-loss-hong-kong-intl-hnk> <https://www.theguardian.com/technology/article/2024/may/17/uk-engineering-arup-deepfake-scam-hong-kong-ai-video>

### step-4: Approximately US$25.6M lost (impact)

Arup disclosed the loss and said its internal IT systems were not compromised.

# LLMjacking via stolen cloud credentials (Sysdig)

- ID: llmjacking-sysdig-2024-05
- Reported: 2024-05-06
- AI role: ai_credential_theft
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/llmjacking-sysdig-2024-05/

## Summary
After a Laravel CVE-2021-3129 foothold, attackers stole cloud credentials and probed ten AI services (AI21, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure, ElevenLabs, MakerSuite, Mistral, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and GCP Vertex) to resell LLM access via reverse proxies while victims paid inference bills. Later Sysdig reporting showed 85,000+ Bedrock requests with Converse API abuse within 30 days of launch. Pillar Security separately reported the Bizarre Bazaar campaign targeting AI startups for unauthorized inference resale.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: Vulnerable Laravel (CVE-2021-3129) leading to cloud credential theft
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: Potential >$46,000/day Claude 2.x costs cited; July 2024 spike 61k Bedrock requests in 3 hours

## Attack flow
### step-1: Vulnerable Laravel provides a foothold (access)

The report identifies CVE-2021-3129 before credential theft.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack> <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/growing-dangers-of-llmjacking>

### step-2: Cloud credentials are stolen (execution)

Attackers obtain keys and probe multiple AI providers.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack> <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/growing-dangers-of-llmjacking>

### step-3: Inference access is proxied (ai)

Authorized model access is resold through attacker reverse proxies.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack> <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/growing-dangers-of-llmjacking>

### step-4: Victim accounts incur inference usage (impact)

The report describes high-volume requests and potentially substantial costs.

Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack> <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/growing-dangers-of-llmjacking>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0012](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0012) Valid Accounts — Stolen cloud credentials are used to access inference services.
  Evidence: <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack> <https://www.sysdig.com/blog/growing-dangers-of-llmjacking>

## Prevention
Monitor Bedrock ListFoundationModels+Invoke/Converse from long-term AKIA keys; rotate exposed keys; SCP restrict Bedrock

## Detections
- Monitor AWS Bedrock API abuse (guidance) — Alert on unusual Bedrock ListFoundationModels, InvokeModel, and Converse API calls, especially from AKIA long-term keys. Monitor for spike patterns (e.g., 61k requests in 3 hours). Implement CloudTrail analysis for Bedrock usage from unexpected geolocations or IAM principals.
- Detect stolen cloud credentials (guidance) — Scan for exposed AWS keys in public repositories, logs, and error tracking services. Rotate credentials immediately upon detection. Use SCPs to restrict Bedrock access to approved principals only.

## Timeline
- First seen: 2024-05-06
- Last updated: 2026-11-05
- 2024-05-06 (Sysdig): Initial LLMjacking disclosure; Laravel CVE-2021-3129 to cloud credential theft and AI inference resale
- 2024-07-01 (Sysdig): Bedrock Converse API abuse observed; 85k+ requests within 30 days of launch
- 2026-01-28 (Pillar Security): Bizarre Bazaar campaign targets AI startups with LLMjacking
- 2026-09-03 (FortiGuard): AWS Bedrock Marketplace abuse; attackers subscribe victims to high-cost models without approval
- 2026-09-09 (Okta Security): Stolen AI session tokens enable LLMjacking without long-term credentials; bypasses MFA and key rotation

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- [AWS Bedrock](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/) [Claude](https://claude.com/product/overview) v2/v3
- OpenAI
- Anthropic
- Azure
- [Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai)
- others in probe list

### Other tooling
- LLM reverse proxy for resale

## Source notes
2026 updates expand LLMjacking scope: Bedrock Marketplace abuse (FortiGuard), AI startup targeting (Pillar Bizarre Bazaar), and session token theft (Okta)

## Sources
- [Sysdig: LLMjacking - Stolen Cloud Credentials Used in New AI Attack](https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack)
- [Sysdig: Growing Dangers of LLMjacking](https://www.sysdig.com/blog/growing-dangers-of-llmjacking)
- [Pillar Security: Bizarre Bazaar - LLMjacking Campaign Targeting AI Startups](https://www.pillar.io/blog/bizarre-bazaar-llmjacking-jan-2026)

# Unit 42: LLMs obfuscating malicious JavaScript

- ID: unit42-llm-js-obfuscation-2024
- Reported: 2024-05-01
- AI role: llm_generated_malware
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/unit42-llm-js-obfuscation-2024/

## Summary
Showed LLMs can effectively rewrite and obfuscate existing malicious JavaScript to evade detection, while finding fully AI-written malware from scratch less practical at the time.

Evidence qualification: Research demonstration of LLM obfuscation efficacy; not a single named campaign.

## Category

## Attribution

- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

The experiment starts with existing code rather than an observed delivery campaign.

Evidence: <https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/using-llms-obfuscate-malicious-javascript/>

### step-2: LLMs rewrite and obfuscate the code (ai)

Model output changes the script while retaining malicious behavior.

Evidence: <https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/using-llms-obfuscate-malicious-javascript/>

### step-3: Researchers test detection outcomes (execution)

The study compares detection before and after rewriting.

Evidence: <https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/using-llms-obfuscate-malicious-javascript/>

### step-4: Demo measures evasion (impact)

The finding concerns obfuscation efficacy, not a separate confirmed victim intrusion.

# Morris II generative AI email worm (research PoC)

- ID: morris-ii-ai-worm-poc-2024-03
- Reported: 2024-03-01
- AI role: ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/morris-ii-ai-worm-poc-2024-03/

## Summary
Adversarial self-replicating prompts make GenAI email assistants propagate malicious instructions to other agents (zero-click in lab), with potential spam/exfil side effects. Tested against GPT-4, Gemini Pro, LLaVA in controlled setups.

Evidence qualification: Controlled research PoC against GenAI-powered email assistants; not observed in the wild.

## Category
attacks-on-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
unverified

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: Research payload enters an email assistant (access)

The controlled experiment places adversarial content in assistant-readable email.

Evidence: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817> <https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/>

### step-2: Self-replicating instructions are processed (ai)

The model follows a prompt designed to reproduce itself.

Evidence: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817> <https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/>

### step-3: Assistant propagates the payload (execution)

Generated email carries the adversarial instructions to another assistant.

Evidence: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817> <https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/>

### step-4: Lab demonstrates propagation (impact)

Potential spam and data-exfiltration effects are research outcomes, not confirmed real-world victims.

Evidence: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817> <https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0051.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0051.001) Indirect — Email content injects instructions into assistants in a controlled experiment.
  Evidence: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817> <https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/>
- [AML.T0061](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0061) LLM Prompt Self-Replication — The prompt is designed to replicate into assistant output.
  Evidence: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817> <https://www.wired.com/story/here-come-the-ai-worms/>

## Prevention
Treat retrieved email/content as untrusted; isolation between agent mailboxes

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in Morris II generative AI email worm (research PoC). Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

- [LLaVA](https://github.com/haotian-liu/LLaVA)
- RAG email assistants

### Other tooling
- unknown

unknown

# BlackMamba AI-synthesized polymorphic keylogger (PoC)

- ID: hyas-blackmamba-poc-2023-08
- Reported: 2023-08-01
- AI role: llm_generated_malware
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/hyas-blackmamba-poc-2023-08/

## Summary
PoC that calls an LLM API to generate unique in-memory keylogger code each run via Python exec and exfiltrates via Microsoft Teams webhooks; claimed to evade an industry EDR with zero alerts in demo.

Evidence qualification: Landmark PoC published ~Aug 2023 (just before Oct 2023 window). Included as frequently cited precursor; not in-the-wild.

## Category
adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
unverified

## Scope and targeting
- Initial access: unknown
- Victims and sectors: unknown
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

## Attack flow
### step-1: Research execution starts in a lab (unknown)

This is a proof of concept, with no established in-the-wild initial access.

Evidence: <https://www.hyas.com/blog/blackmamba-using-ai-to-generate-polymorphic-malware>

### step-2: LLM synthesizes keylogger code (ai)

An API call returns a new in-memory payload at runtime.

Evidence: <https://www.hyas.com/blog/blackmamba-using-ai-to-generate-polymorphic-malware>

### step-3: Python executes the generated code (execution)

The PoC evaluates the returned code in memory.

Evidence: <https://www.hyas.com/blog/blackmamba-using-ai-to-generate-polymorphic-malware>

### step-4: Demo exfiltrates through Teams (impact)

The research uses Teams webhooks to demonstrate data exfiltration.

Evidence: <https://www.hyas.com/blog/blackmamba-using-ai-to-generate-polymorphic-malware>

### Connections

- step-1 -> step-2
- step-2 -> step-3
- step-3 -> step-4

## MITRE ATLAS
- [AML.T0102](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0102) Generate Malicious Commands — The proof of concept dynamically generates keylogger code through a model API.
  Evidence: <https://www.hyas.com/blog/blackmamba-using-ai-to-generate-polymorphic-malware>

## Prevention
EDR behavioral on Teams webhook exfil; block unexpected generative API from endpoints

## Detections
- Review attack-specific indicators (guidance) — Monitor for the techniques described in BlackMamba AI-synthesized polymorphic keylogger (PoC). Refer to sources for specific IOCs and TTPs.

## Timeline
No timeline is recorded.

## Tools
### AI tooling and models
- OpenAI-style LLM API

- [Python](https://github.com/python/cpython) exec
- Microsoft Teams webhooks

# Android malware posing as ChatGPT apps

- ID: unit42-android-chatgpt-malware-2023
- Reported: 2023-03-21
- AI role: ai_tool_as_lure
- Entry: https://openattacks.ai/attacks/unit42-android-chatgpt-malware-2023/

## Summary
Android APKs impersonating ChatGPT delivered Meterpreter and SMS-fraud malware. Broader ChatGPT-themed phishing and trojan sites rose with GenAI popularity.

adversary-use-of-ai

## Attribution
unknown

## AI involvement confidence
confirmed

- Victims and sectors: Android users seeking ChatGPT apps
- Regions: unknown
- Region notes: unknown
- Scale and metrics: unknown

Phishing or trojan sites offer Android APKs.

The application impersonates the AI product.

### step-3: User sideloads the APK (execution)

The package delivers Meterpreter or SMS-fraud malware.

### step-4: Remote access or SMS fraud (impact)

The reported payload determines the resulting device abuse.
